newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania inmates demand new laws, end to squalor.
newsitem.headline: Romania inmates demand new laws, end to squalor.

text.p: Thousands of inmates, some sleeping three to a bed, intensified a protest on Wednesday in Bucharest's main prison to demand better conditions and faster parole and were joined by convicts in a second jail.
Inmates at the 19th century prison on the capital's outskirts refused food, burned bedsheets and shouted "Freedom, freedom," and "We want new laws" for the third day in a row.

"We will go to the bitter end with our protests," Constantin Vasiliu, one of 3,500 convicts in the Bucharest prison, told Reuters in Cell No. 56. The room was jammed with 51 inmates, three times normal capacity.
Unshaven inmates stuck their heads through the narrow windows of steel cell doors, shouting: "We want our rights".
The prison, intended to hold 1,500 inmates, is typical in a country where post-Communist crime has swelled the numbers of those serving time.
Official statistics say there are 43,000 inmates in Romania, but a spokesman for the Justice Ministry's Department of Jails put the number of those in temporary or long-term custody at up to 100,000.
"There has been no violence," prison warden Ion Pirjol said in his office. "So far we have kept up a constant dialogue."
In Craiova, 200 km (120 miles) southwest of Bucharest, 2,500 inmates launched a noisy sympathy protest.
"This is a chain reaction," Craiova jail warden Colonel Gheorghe Lazaroiu said by telephone. "The situation is quite tense here. A spark would be enough to start violence."
The prisoners are demanding the repeal of amendments last year to the criminal code extending the detention period to qualify for parole from one-half to two-thirds of a sentence.
Prisoners demand more family visits and complain about poor sanitation, with two latrines for several dozen people. They say conditions breed disease, violence and homosexual assaults.
The 1989 overthrow of communism spawned a dramatic rise in serious crime and substantial cutbacks in funding for all public services, with jails a low priority.
"The problem is serious," Pirjol said. "There are plans to build new prisons but this is a project wich will take some time and funds to be completed."
In cell No. 56, 51 inmates shared 20 beds standing in three tiers up to the ceiling.

"We live like worms here," said one prisoner, a slight man in his forties. "Now you understand why anyone would go mad. I see the same faces for months and years. I know that I can be easy prey for any homosexual here."
